overview: Between 1300 and 1492 this atlas label covers parts of Borneo and southwestern Sulawesi. It is regional shorthand, not one kingdom or a reliable description of everyone’s religion. In South Sulawesi, growing rice production and overseas exchange helped local ruling communities develop into larger kingdoms. Their histories belong beside, rather than inside, the story of any single distant empire.

periods.title: Rice fields and growing centres
periods.summary: Soppeng researchers connect fourteenth-century political growth with expanding lowland rice farming.

periods.title: Island connections
periods.summary: A Javanese court poem of 1365 names Makassar and Bantaeng; this is an external claim, not proof of direct government throughout the islands.

periods.title: Regional societies continue
periods.summary: Agricultural kingdoms and their networks persisted beyond the atlas endpoint; they did not all end together.

items.text: The decoded outlines include Soppeng, Gowa, Bantaeng and the Mahakam region around Kutai Lama. They exclude Java, Bali and western Sarawak. The similarly named earlier states record mostly covers Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, while another minor-kingdoms label includes India. None is a substitute for these island communities’ own history.

Kutai Lama stood beside the Mahakam River in eastern Borneo. Later Kutai tradition places a royal centre there around 1300. That traditional starting date should not be confused with a securely dated foundation inscription, or with the much earlier Muara Kaman inscriptions upstream. Different places and periods lie behind the familiar name Kutai.

Researchers interpreting Sewo in Soppeng describe a shift from hill settlements toward gentler lowlands suited to rice fields. Their explanation links systematic cultivation and food surpluses with the joining of farming villages into a kingdom during the fourteenth century. Political change was also a change in where people worked and lived.

At Allangkanangnge, a former Bugis palace site, researchers recovered microscopic silica traces from rice husks. These phytoliths survive after the plant has gone. Combined with ceramics, they provide direct evidence for rice in the development of agrarian kingdoms. A rice plant can leave a clue much smaller than a grain.

From around 1300, clearing forest, directing water and building embanked rice fields demanded coordinated labour in South Sulawesi. Farmers also faced insects, rodents and hungry birds. More rice could support more people and trade, but harvests did not become automatic just because a ruler wanted a surplus.

River and lake communities could obtain fish, salt and edible plants as well as grain. Rivers such as the Saddang and Jeneberrang served as routes between settlements. This environmental setting helps explain why fields, fishing places and waterways mattered together, instead of reducing every family’s food to a bowl of rice.

Just outside the atlas’s southern Borneo outline, Patih Muhur offers a useful building comparison. Archaeologists found shaped ironwood posts with square holes for crosspieces; supporting logs and smaller wooden braces helped stop them sinking into wet ground. Keeping a heavy structure upright in soft soil required more than simply planting a tree trunk.

One Patih Muhur wood test was reported as a broad medieval age, but its relationship to later historical accounts is unresolved. The excavator called for more samples and improved analysis. The braced timbers are real; their precise date and identification with a named kingdom’s port remain questions.

South Sulawesi kingdoms drew authority from descent groups that recognized both parental lines. Some joined several such groups in alliances. Kinship could therefore shape who ruled and who supported a ruler. This describes political organization; it does not tell us that every household had the same size or daily routine.

A later Soppeng genealogy remembers Wé Tékéwanua as a woman ruler and links her family’s marriages with neighbouring lands. It also credits her with encouraging rice planting. Historian Stephen Druce warns that the earliest generations rely on oral tradition. The account reveals how later people remembered women and family alliances in royal history.

Bulu Matanre in Soppeng had stone defenses protecting a mountain pass. Archaeologists place its occupation broadly between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries. Not every nearby hill settlement was fortified. Controlling a route offers a practical explanation for this wall without making every fortress the result of the same drought or war.

At Kutai, rivers linked several successive centres rather than one unchanging capital. Archaeological collections contain ceramics, beads, coins, sculpture and animal remains from different periods. These objects reveal many kinds of activity, but a museum display assembled today is not a photograph of a single medieval family’s belongings.

A later Bugis historical text opens, in scholarly Roman transcription, Iana sureq poadaqadaqéngngi tanaé ri Soppéng: “This is the writing that tells of the land of Soppéng.” Ian Caldwell records this wording in manuscript versions studied for his 1988 thesis. The text appeared in Bugis script in Matthes’s 1864 collection; this is a later written witness, not a surviving page from 1300.

The Soppeng history was probably first written down in the eighteenth century. Its remembered place names nevertheless helped researchers investigate older settlements. Written tradition and archaeology can ask questions of each other: a story suggests where to look, while pottery can test how old occupation there actually was.

Later Bugis manuscripts preserved calendars, diaries, genealogies and religious or historical works as well as poetry. Surviving collections often contain copies commissioned in the nineteenth century. Copying and comparing texts preserved knowledge, but the date of a surviving book must be distinguished from the age of the events it describes.

For a clearly later example of literary skill, Colliq Pujie, Queen Mother of Tanete, copied a major Bugis La Galigo manuscript in the nineteenth century. Leiden preserves its twelve volumes. A woman’s sustained scholarly work helped transmit an enormous epic; the physical books are centuries later than this map interval.

ending.text: 1492 is an atlas stopping point, not a shared conquest. South Sulawesi’s kingdoms continued; Goa and Talloq became major powers in the sixteenth century, and Islam spread among Bugis and Makasar communities around 1600. Borneo’s centres followed other histories. Political and religious change did not erase their communities or languages.
